transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-10-21
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: 52m
Attendees: Samantha Lee (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Priya Kaur (Redwood Product), Jenna Patel (MiraWell Head of Platform), Marcus Li (MiraWell SRE), Elena Ruiz (MiraWell CTO), Aisha Noor (MiraWell Privacy)
Recording link: https://redwood.app/rec/ff-20251021-9b3f (shared)

Summary:
Quick Console walkthrough focused on request playback, trace correlation between request logs and model requests, error root cause investigation patterns, and options for both Hosted and Private deployments. Customer wanted to understand how to debug falling latencies, model fallback behaviours, and how KMS/audit logs surface in the Console.

Topics Covered:
- Request playback / Request Inspector demo
- Trace <-> log stitching and correlation ids
- KV cache and fallback semantics when cache misses escalate cost/latency
- Private/VPC telemetry and audit logging exposure
- SSO, audit logs, and KMS integration overview

--- Transcript Body (timestamps approximate) ---
00:00 Samantha: okay everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros, i'm Samantha from Redwood AE, we have Diego who will drive the console today, and Priya from product. Jenna, do you want to kick off with what you're seeing?
00:22 Jenna: sure, um we have sporadic spikes where chatbot responses take 1.2 to 2.5s longer, and sometimes the model falls back to a smaller variant. we'd like to understand why, and how to trace it back to infra or request patterns.
00:38 Diego: totally. we'll show the Request Inspector flow, request playback, and how traces are stitched to infra logs. the console calls it Request Inspector, but sometimes in our notes folks see 'Sherlock' or trace inspector, so sorry if names mix.
:52 Marcus: ha yeah i saw a doc that said 'sherlock', so made sense. our priority is: reproducible debugging and low-noise alerts.
01:03 Diego: great. first i'll pull up the console — top nav, Request logs. i'm switching to example workspace that mirrors your production schema.
01:21 Samantha: quick note on tenancy — since MiraWell is evaluating both Hosted and Private, the console surface is mostly the same; Private just wires the telemetry to your VPC and your KMS for keys.
01:34 Diego: ok i'm clicking into a request that shows a 2.3s jump. timestamped trace on the right, request timeline on the left. you can see prefix cache hit/miss, batching window, and kernel selection steps.
01:50 Diego: (pointing) here the KV-cache says miss at 0.12s, then a batch formed at 0.48s, then model fallback at 0.9s — fallback to small-quantized variant. the console annotates where the runtime switched kernels — sometimes that shows as 'quant exec' or spelled weird in transcript output.
02:12 Marcus: can we see the upstream request payload so we can confirm prompt length distribution?
02:18 Diego: yes — expanding request shows the raw prompt and token counts. also shows any pre- and post-processing hooks we run. that's helpful to know whether long prompts caused recompile or batching delays.
02:40 Jenna: what's the correlation id between our app logs and this console trace? how do we map them?
02:46 Diego: good question. there's a request_id we return in the API and we recommend passing your own request_id header. the console will show both — if you paste your app log request_id into the search bar, it will stitch the traces. see the 'linked logs' panel — clicking opens the original log context (we fetch last 100 log lines).
03:10 Marcus: what about privacy — will those logs contain PII? Aisha: yes this is a big question for us.
03:18 Aisha: we need to ensure only redacted logs go across hosted. we can't send PHI outside our VPC for production.
03:25 Samantha: understood — for Private deployments we can route telemetry to your VPC and you can enable redaction rules in the agent. for hosted, there are field-level redaction and retention controls; we'll include the security doc with exact retention windows.
03:44 Diego: switching to a different example — here is a failure mode where cache thrash causes repeated model reloads. the console shows 'evict>reload' events, and you can replay the entire request sequence in the playback pane.
04:02 Diego: i'll hit replay — note the playback speed controls, and the option to step frame-by-frame so you can see the interleaving of logs and model calls. that helps when looking at a 500 or 504 that originates from an upstream timeout.
04:22 Elena: on fallbacks — when the runtime chooses a cheaper variant, does it preserve output shape and function calls?
04:28 Diego: mostly yes, we map function schemas, but there can be differences especially with quantized variants. the console flags 'compatibility warnings' when a fallback might change tokenization or function calling semantics. for critical paths we recommend 'pinned version' or 'canary then fallback' policies that Redwood supports.
04:55 Marcus: any metrics we can alert on that are good predictors of degradations?
05:00 Priya: we have pre-baked SLO charts: batching window percentiles, cache hit ratio, model-switch counts, tail latency (99.9). console can emit those to your alerting endpoint; we also show correlated recent config changes.
05:18 Samantha: Diego, can you show a security/audit log sample? Jenna wants to see where KMS key ops show up.
05:24 Diego: yep — audit logs pane. here you can filter by user, API key, or KMS key alias. operations like "model deploy", "key rotation", "role change" are logged. for Private, you can pipe these logs into your SIEM.
05:40 Jenna: ok that looks good — will that be sufficient for our audit team or do we need more?
05:44 Samantha: we'll send the SOC2 pack. in addition, we have an architecture note for the Private deployment that outlines what telemetry stays in your VPC and what the control plane sees.
05:58 Marcus: can we run a live replay against a canary model to reproduce the regression in our environment? we want deterministic replay.
06:06 Diego: yes — two options: 1) Console-based replay where we run the exact request through the hosted runtime (good for quick repro), 2) an isolated replay harness we can deploy into your Private environment to run against pinned model artifacts and your infra. the second respects your encryption and network rules.
06:30 Jenna: for option 2, what is the onboarding delta? we don't want another heavy install.
06:35 Diego: it's a small containerized harness plus a tiny agent that grabs artifacts from your S3. takes a couple of hours to wire up, then you can replay at scale. we'll provide a deployment guide.
06:48 Samantha: i want to highlight the trace -> log stitching again: when you provide your app's request_id we can show the precise trace row where KV cache missed and the batching decision happened; that helps pinpoint whether it's app-side bursts or runtime scheduling.
07:05 Marcus: about scheduling — is batching always beneficial? sometimes we suffer when small interactive requests hit batching windows.
07:12 Diego: it's a tradeoff — the console suggests per-route policies. you can set an aggressive low-latency route (no batching, higher cost), or a bulk route that uses batching aggressively. Optimize will suggest defaults based on your token distribution.
07:30 Elena: any tooling to simulate high concurrency to validate autoscale?
07:34 Priya: yes, we have a stress runner script and a sandbox test harness. Diego can run a quick load test in the lab session.
07:44 Diego: i'll demo a small load-run: launching now — you'll see a spike, console will show autoscale ramp and the model warmup times, plus any fallback events.
08:05 Diego: ok here's an example incident: a sequence where upstream auth latencies spiked, client re-tried, requests pile up, batch grew, kernel recompile started at high token length and that pushed median up. console highlights the chain: "upstream -> retries -> larger batching -> kernel select -> latency tail".
08:34 Jenna: that's perfect, can we have a cookbook for triage steps? like, check request_id -> inspect prefix cache -> check kernel select -> check model variant?
08:41 Samantha: yes we have a runbook. i'll add it to the follow-up email.
08:48 Marcus: one more: what about multi-region fallbacks? we can't cross region for data residency.
08:53 Diego: policy-based routing handles region constraints — we can only route to permitted regions. if a region is unhealthy we have config to fail closed vs fallback to an allowed region. that latter only for non-PII routes.
09:12 Aisha: confirm: keys used for request encryption in Private are your customer's KMS, not Redwood's?
09:17 Samantha: correct — in Private, KMS/HSM is customer-managed. hosted can use customer-managed keys (bring-your-own) via cloud KMS integrations. we'll put exact steps in the security pack.
09:30 Diego: moving on, i'll show the error analysis panel — when a model returns an error we capture model stderr, runtime error codes, and the exact token index where it failed. the console surfaces common root causes and a suggested remediation.
09:52 Jenna: sometimes our logs show 504s with no model errors — is that a routing issue?
09:57 Diego: could be. console correlates 504s with upstream traces, network latencies, and internal queue overflows. you can expand the event timeline to see the queue length and memory usage at the time.
10:15 Marcus: what's the retention of request logs in hosted? can we extend?
10:19 Samantha: default 30 days, can be extended as an add-on to 1 year. Private you control retention fully.
10:30 Jenna: ok great. last thing — we want to validate that our privacy team signs off before demoing internal PII logs to Redwood. can we do the lab without sharing PII?
10:38 Samantha: absolutely, you can scrub or use synthetic traces. Diego's replay harness can operate on sanitized payloads.
10:46 Diego: wrapping up demo — key takeaways: request playback + trace stitching gives deterministic debugging; playback harness supports Private replay; audit logs & KMS available for compliance; pre-built SLO charts and Optimize recommendations aid routing/batch tradeoffs.
11:08 Samantha: let's do next steps: i'll send the security pack and runbook, Diego will schedule the 2-hour lab, Jenna will share sample failing IDs. any final Qs?
11:20 Elena: can you include an estimated cost delta for enabling low-latency routes?
11:25 Samantha: yes i'll include a cost delta table in the follow-up.
11:30 Jenna: thanks everyone, that was helpful. we'll review and aim to pick dates for the lab.
11:36 Samantha: thanks all — we'll follow up by Thursday.
